title: Effects of correlated color temperature of light on thermal comfort, thermophysiology and cognitive performance
research_question: This study investigated the effects of correlated color temperature (CCT) of light in an office-like scenario with relatively long exposure durations (>2 h) on 1) visual perceptions and eye-related symptoms, 2) thermal perceptions, 3) thermophysiology, 4) cognitive performance, and 5) alertness, pleasure and arousal, under mild cold exposure (17 °C).

participants.description: 16 Caucasian participants (8 males, 8 females), aged 18-40 years old (mean 23.7 ± 4.1 y), BMI 18-27.5 kg/m² (mean 21.9 ± 2.3 kg/m²), normal chronotype, non-smokers, no color blindness, healthy, living in the Netherlands. Females on hormonal contraception.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Two constant CCT conditions (2700 K and 5700 K) in an office-like, windowless room. Illuminance was kept constant at 500 lux at eye level. Ambient air temperature was 17.2 ± 0.3 °C (mild cold), mean radiant temperature 17.2 ± 0.2 °C, relative humidity 40-48%, air speed 0.15-0.26 m/s. Each exposure lasted 140 minutes.

mechanisms: Hue-heat hypothesis (visual mechanism): blue colors are perceived as cooler, red/yellow as warmer. (Not supported for thermal sensation in this study).

Non-visual effects (via intrinsically photoreceptive retinal ganglion cells - ipRGCs): higher CCT leads to increased arousal/alertness, physiological changes (e.g., energy expenditure, decreased shivering), which can affect thermal comfort and cognitive performance. These effects build up over longer exposure durations.
Visual comfort: an association between visual comfort and thermal comfort, suggesting a shared underlying drive for comfort.
Cognitive resource modulation: CCT can directly affect cognitive performance via acute alerting effects (non-visual pathway).
Motivation and effort investment: higher CCT increased motivation and effort, which are powerful determinants of complex cognitive performance.
Melanopic illuminance and exposure duration: non-visual responses follow a sigmoid function and require sufficient exposure duration to manifest.
moderators: Exposure duration (for non-visual effects and some subjective perceptions)
Ambient temperature (mild cold vs. warm conditions)
Illuminance (though fixed in this study, acknowledged as a moderator in literature)
implementation_implications: High CCT (5700 K) can enhance thermal comfort, alertness, arousal, pleasure, and comprehensive cognitive performance in mild cold office-like conditions.
Adjusting CCT of light requires nearly no extra energy in most color-tunable lighting systems, offering a sustainable way to improve indoor environmental quality.
The effects of CCT on thermal comfort are likely mediated by non-visual mechanisms that build up over longer exposure durations, rather than immediate visual (hue-heat) effects.
The hue-heat hypothesis was not supported for thermal sensation in mild cold conditions, suggesting its applicability may be limited by context or individual differences.
Future studies should investigate CCT effects in various populations, contexts (e.g., warm conditions), and with long-term exposures to understand adaptation.

limitations: The study only tested CCT effects in mild cold conditions (17 °C), so results may not generalize to warm conditions.

The hue-heat hypothesis was not supported, potentially due to large inter-individual variation in color-temperature associations among participants, and cannot exclude its existence in other populations or contexts.
The color-temperature association may be dynamic and change with repeated exposure, which was not investigated.
Only one illuminance level (500 lux) was tested, limiting the ability to investigate interactions between CCT and illuminance.
Participants were engaged in screen activity, which might have reduced their awareness of the ambient light color appearance.
